lead: A zero-knowledge proof lets one party, the prover, convince another, the verifier, that a statement is true without handing over the evidence. The verifier learns only one bit: the statement is true. This is useful when the evidence is a secret, such as a password, a private key, or a colouring of a graph. The idea appears in privacy-preserving login, anonymous credentials and blockchain systems, where you must prove you are allowed to act without revealing why.
prereq: You need one-way functions from Chapter 4.1 and hash commitments from Chapter 4.6; a little probability for the soundness error.

blocks.text: A zero-knowledge proof is an interactive protocol between a prover P and a verifier V. P knows a secret witness w for a public statement x. The statement might be “this graph has a 3-colouring” and w is the colouring. The protocol must satisfy three properties.
Completeness: if the statement is true and P follows the protocol, V accepts with probability 1, or very close to 1. An honest prover always convinces an honest verifier.

Soundness: if the statement is false, no cheating prover can make V accept, except with a small probability called the soundness error. For one round of the 3-colouring protocol the error is at most 1 − 1/|E|, where |E| is the number of edges in the graph. Repeating r independent rounds drives the error to at most (1 − 1/|E|)^r.

Zero knowledge: V learns nothing beyond the truth of x. Formally, there is a simulator S that, using only x and V’s randomness, can produce a transcript that looks exactly like a real run with P. If such a simulator exists, the transcript carries no secret information.

Honest-verifier zero knowledge is the weaker version most courses state: the simulator works only when V follows the protocol and does not deviate. It does not protect against a verifier who chooses challenges maliciously.

Take a graph G = (V, E). The public statement is: G has a 3-colouring. The secret witness is a colouring c: V → {1, 2, 3} in which the two ends of every edge have different colours. A commitment is a hash H(colour || r) with a random nonce r; it hides the colour and binds the prover to it.

items: The prover picks a random permutation π of {1, 2, 3}. For each vertex v it computes the hidden colour π(c(v)), picks a fresh nonce r_v, and sends com_v = H(π(c(v)) || r_v) to the verifier.
The verifier picks one edge (u, v) uniformly from E and sends it as the challenge.
The prover opens only the two commitments for u and v: it sends π(c(u)), r_u, π(c(v)), r_v.
The verifier recomputes the two hashes, checks they match the commitments, and accepts the round when the two opened colours differ.
Both sides repeat r independent rounds. The prover must reshuffle and recommit every round.

blocks.where: |E| is the number of edges; the verifier picks one edge uniformly and at least one edge is monochromatic.
r is the number of independent rounds; each round uses a fresh permutation and fresh commitments.

blocks.text: Why it leaks nothing: each round opens one edge under a fresh random permutation. The verifier sees two different colours, which is exactly what any valid edge looks like; it never sees the original colour labels or the unopened vertices. Commitments are hiding, so unopened colours stay secret, and binding stops the prover from changing a colour after seeing the challenge.

The Fiat–Shamir transform removes the live verifier. The prover computes the challenge itself as e = H(statement || all commitments), where H is a cryptographic hash. The prover then sends the commitments and responses. Anyone can recompute e and check the proof. This makes the proof non-interactive; security is argued in the random-oracle model, where H behaves like a random function.

The 3-colouring protocol is one example. Graph isomorphism proves that two graphs are the same up to renaming vertices without revealing the mapping. Schnorr’s protocol proves knowledge of a discrete logarithm without revealing the exponent. Both use the same commit–challenge–respond pattern.

items: Password-free login: prove you hold a private key or password-derived secret without sending it.
Blockchain privacy: prove a transaction is valid without revealing sender, receiver or amount.
Cloud correctness: prove a remote server computed the promised result without sending all the data.
Anonymous credentials: prove you are over 18 or hold a valid permit without showing the full document.

examples.question: A triangle graph has vertices A, B, C and edges AB, BC, CA. The prover claims it has a 3-colouring. (a) Show an honest prover using colours 1, 2, 3 on A, B, C passes one round. (b) A cheating prover has only colours 1 and 2. Find its pass probability for one round. (c) Find the probability it passes 10 independent rounds. (d) State the general soundness bound for a graph with |E| edges and r rounds.
steps: Label the triangle vertices A, B, C. The edges are AB, BC, CA, so |E| = 3.
Honest colouring: A = 1, B = 2, C = 3. Edge AB has colours 1 and 2, BC has 2 and 3, CA has 3 and 1. All three edges have different endpoint colours.
A random permutation of {1, 2, 3} keeps all endpoint colours different, so the honest prover passes every round with probability 1.
Cheating prover with only colours 1 and 2: by the pigeonhole principle, two of the three vertices get the same colour. Those two vertices form exactly one edge. That edge is monochromatic.
The other two edges have different colours. The verifier picks one of the 3 edges uniformly. The prover passes only if the verifier picks one of the two good edges, so P(pass) = 2/3 = 0.6667.
In 10 independent rounds the prover must pass each round. P(pass all 10) = (2/3)^10 = 1024/59049 = 0.01734.
General bound: for |E| = m edges and r rounds, P(pass all) ≤ (1 − 1/m)^r; substituting m = 3, r = 10 gives (2/3)^10.
examples.answer: The cheating prover passes one round with probability 0.6667 and ten independent rounds with probability 0.01734, so the soundness error is under 2 percent.

traps: Do not say zero knowledge means the verifier learns nothing at all; the verifier does learn that the statement is true.
Do not swap soundness and completeness. Completeness is about an honest prover passing; soundness is about a cheating prover failing.
Do not forget that the prover must reshuffle and recommit every round. Reusing one commitment lets the verifier collect many opened edges and rebuild the colouring.
For the triangle with only two colours, exactly one of the three edges is monochromatic. The pass probability is 2/3, not 1/3 and not 1/2.

quiz.q: State completeness, soundness and zero knowledge in one sentence each.
quiz.a: Completeness: an honest prover convinces an honest verifier. Soundness: a cheating prover fails except with small probability. Zero knowledge: the verifier learns nothing beyond the truth of the statement.

quiz.q: Why must the prover use a fresh random permutation and fresh commitments in every round?
quiz.a: If one commitment is reused, the verifier can ask for different edges in different rounds. The opened colours then belong to the same hidden colouring, and the verifier can combine them to rebuild the full colouring. A fresh permutation makes each opened edge independent of the others.

quiz.q: A cheating prover for a triangle graph with only two colours runs 5 independent rounds. Find the probability it passes all five.
quiz.a: Per round the pass probability is 2/3. For five independent rounds it is (2/3)^5 = 32/243 = 0.1317, about 13.2 percent.

quiz.q: For a graph with |E| = m edges, explain why one round catches a cheating prover with probability at least 1/m. Hence give the r-round soundness error.
quiz.a: Any invalid colouring has at least one monochromatic edge. The verifier picks one edge uniformly from m edges, so it picks a bad edge with probability at least 1/m. The cheat passes one round with probability at most 1 − 1/m. In r independent rounds the pass probability is at most (1 − 1/m)^r.
A protocol is honest-verifier zero knowledge when a simulator can produce a transcript that is indistinguishable from a real run, provided the verifier follows the protocol honestly.

quiz.q: What two properties must a hash commitment have in the 3-colouring protocol?
quiz.a: Hiding: the hash does not reveal the committed colour. Binding: the prover cannot later open the same commitment to a different colour, because that would require finding a different input with the same hash.

quiz.q: In the Fiat–Shamir transform, how is the verifier’s challenge replaced, and why does the proof become non-interactive?
quiz.a: The challenge is replaced by e = H(statement || all commitments). The prover computes e from public data and sends the responses. Any verifier can recompute e and check the proof, so no live challenge message is needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems use zk-SNARKs and zk-STARKs, which make the proof short enough to post on a blockchain. Bulletproofs give short proofs without a trusted setup. Anonymous credentials use these ideas to prove attributes such as age or citizenship without showing the document. Search for “zk-SNARK”, “zk-STARK”, “Bulletproofs” and “anonymous credentials” to go further.
